overview: Two thresholds from the same broth dilution experiment — one tells you what stops growth, the other tells you what actually kills.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Minimum Inhibitory Concentration — the lowest antibiotic concentration that visibly inhibits bacterial growth after incubation.
aspects.valueB: Minimum Bactericidal Concentration — the lowest antibiotic concentration that kills at least 99.9% of the original bacterial inoculum.

aspects.label: What It Actually Measures
aspects.valueA: Growth inhibition — bacteria may still be viable but not growing/visible.
aspects.valueB: Actual killing — measured by subculturing onto antibiotic-free media and counting surviving colonies.

aspects.label: Determination Method
aspects.valueA: Read directly from the broth dilution series as the first clear (no visible turbidity) tube/well.
aspects.valueB: Requires subculturing the clear tubes from the MIC test onto agar and counting colonies after further incubation.

aspects.label: Relationship Between the Two Values
aspects.valueA: Always less than or equal to the corresponding MBC for the same drug/organism pair.
aspects.valueB: Always greater than or equal to the corresponding MIC; a large gap suggests tolerance.

aspects.label: What a Wide MBC/MIC Gap Suggests
aspects.valueA: N/A — MIC alone doesn't reveal this relationship.
aspects.valueB: An MBC much higher than the MIC (typically >4-fold) suggests the drug is only bacteriostatic against that organism, or tolerance is present.

aspects.label: Clinical Relevance
aspects.valueA: Guides routine dosing decisions and susceptibility categorization.
aspects.valueB: Particularly relevant in infections needing bactericidal activity, such as endocarditis or infections in neutropenic patients.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Lowest concentration that stops visible growth.
aspects.valueB: Lowest concentration that actually kills the bacteria.
